x: Centripetal force acts towards the centre and keeps a body on a circular path. Centrifugal force is the outward pseudo force felt only in the rotating frame.
t: Discriminate centripetal (real, inward) from centrifugal (pseudo, outward).

x: Force is measured in newtons (N). Pascal is pressure, watt is power and joule is work or energy.
t: Recall the SI unit of each quantity and eliminate the others.

x: Rocket propulsion is Newton's third law: gases are pushed backward and the rocket is pushed forward. Rest until pushed and seat belts show inertia (first law); lift acceleration uses the second law.
t: Check each example against first, second and third law.

x: One joule is the work done when a force of 1 newton moves a body 1 metre, so 1 J = 1 N m. N s is impulse and W s⁻¹ is not work.
t: Recall work = force × displacement to build the unit.

x: One horsepower equals 746 watts. 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ is the electronvolt conversion, a trap figure.
t: Recall 1 hp = 746 W.

x: Option C is incorrect: fluid friction (viscous drag) opposes motion through fluids, it does not assist it. The other three statements about static, rolling and kinetic friction are true.
t: Check each friction type; every friction opposes motion.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the body keeps moving by inertia (first law) while the bus stops, so the passenger lurches forward.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true and R explains A: drawing the hands back increases the time of impact, so the force on the hands drops for the same change in momentum.
t: Recall F = change in momentum ÷ time.

x: Both are true and R explains A: with only conservative forces, KE + PE stays constant, which is exactly what conservation of mechanical energy means.
t: Check whether R restates the cause of A.

x: Statement A is true: an unbalanced force changes the state of motion. Statement B is false: balanced forces produce no change, so uniform velocity continues.
t: Discriminate balanced from unbalanced forces.

x: Both are true: brakes use friction to turn kinetic energy into heat, and friction between belts and pulleys transmits power.
t: Recall the useful applications of friction.

x: I and II are correct action–reaction pairs. III is reversed: a bird pushes air downward and the air pushes the bird upward.
t: Check the direction in each action–reaction pair.

x: All four are correct: mechanical energy is KE + PE, thermal energy comes from molecular motion, KE can be translational or rotational, and PE can be gravitational or elastic.
t: Recall the classification of energy forms.

x: Friction supplies centripetal force on a level road, gravity for satellites, tension for a stone on a string and electrostatic attraction for an electron, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall which real force provides centripetal force in each case.

x: Lever – scissors and see-saw, inclined plane – ramps and wedges, wheel and axle – steering wheel and door knobs, screw jack – lifting cars, giving a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall one everyday example of each simple machine.

x: All four are correct: a generator turns mechanical into electrical, a motor electrical into mechanical, a battery chemical into electrical and a solar cell light into electrical energy.
t: Check each device's input and output energy.

x: Three are advantages: walking, moving and stopping vehicles, and writing or holding. Wear and tear is a disadvantage of friction.
t: Discriminate advantages from disadvantages of friction.

x: Friction opposes relative motion, tension pulls along a rope, the normal force is a perpendicular push and the spring force is Hooke's restoring force, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the defining feature of each contact force.

x: Both are true and R explains A: weight is the gravitational pull of the Earth on a body, and gravity attracts masses towards each other.
t: Check whether R gives the cause of A.

x: All six are correct: dyne, kgf and poundal are force units, 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻² = 10⁵ dyne, weight is in newtons or kgf, and 1 kgf ≈ 9.8 N.
t: Recall force units and their conversions.

x: All four are correct: rest until pushed is the first law, the heavy suitcase and loaded cart show F = ma (second law), and rocket gases show the third law.
t: Check each example against Newton's three laws.

x: Each reaction is equal and opposite: foot–ground pushes the foot forward, gun–bullet pushes the gun back, nail–hammer and apple–Earth, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall that the reaction reverses the direction of the action.

x: The gun recoils backward. By the third law and momentum conservation, the bullet's forward momentum equals the gun's backward momentum.
t: Recall recoil as a third-law effect.

x: The force on the Earth equals the force on the apple, but the Earth's huge mass makes its acceleration very small, not zero.
t: Recall a = F/m; equal force on a huge mass gives tiny acceleration.

x: All four are correct: without external force an isolated system's momentum is conserved in every collision, and an explosion from rest keeps total momentum zero.
t: Recall the law of conservation of linear momentum.

x: Momentum is conserved in both the gun–bullet and rocket–gas systems; the exhaust gains backward and the rocket forward momentum, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Discriminate the whole system from its parts.

x: The bullet's forward momentum equals the gun's backward momentum, so the total stays zero as it was before firing.
t: Recall momentum conservation for a system starting at rest.

x: Both are true: collision principles guide vehicle safety design, and jet engines throw out fast exhaust to create a large momentum change and thrust.
t: Recall the applications of momentum and collisions.

x: The SI unit of work is the joule; erg, eV, calorie and kWh are other units; 1 J = 10⁷ erg and 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the work units and their conversion factors.

x: All three are correct: sound, light, electrical, magnetic and nuclear are energy forms, an LED turns electrical into light, and a nuclear plant turns nuclear into heat then electricity.
t: Check each energy conversion chain.

x: All three convert potential into kinetic energy: a falling body, a swinging pendulum and a roller coaster going down.
t: Recall examples of PE turning into KE.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the law of conservation of energy says energy only changes form, which is why it cannot be created or destroyed.
t: Check whether R is the law behind A.

x: All four show conservation of mechanical energy: a pendulum, free fall, a spring-mass system and ideal (elastic) collisions.
t: Recall the standard examples of mechanical energy conservation.

x: Both are true: power is measured in watts, 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹, and horsepower, kilowatt and megawatt are other power units.
t: Recall power = work ÷ time and its units.

x: Static friction is self-adjusting, its maximum is μₛN, kinetic friction is μₖN, and rolling friction opposes rolling, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Discriminate static, limiting, kinetic and rolling friction.

x: Friction gives the forward push in walking, grip between pen and paper, grip that stops objects slipping and power transmission in belts, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
t: Recall the role friction plays in each activity.

x: All four are disadvantages of friction: unwanted heat, lower machine efficiency, extra fuel use and surfaces wearing rough over time.
t: Recall the disadvantages of friction.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the inward centripetal force is real because it supplies the centripetal acceleration needed for circular motion.
t: Check whether R gives the role that makes A true.

x: All five can supply centripetal force: tension (stone on string), gravity (satellite), friction (car on curve), electrostatic (electron) and magnetic force (charged particle in a field).
t: Recall which real force acts in each circular motion.

x: Both are true: on a banked road the normal-force component plus friction gives the centripetal force, and in a loop-the-loop gravity plus the normal force does.
t: Check the forces acting in each case.

x: All eight are correct: outward effects in washing machines, wheels, merry-go-rounds, centrifuges, planetary rings and the Earth's equatorial bulge come from the centrifugal pseudo force.
t: Recall centrifugal force as a pseudo force in rotating frames.

x: Gears convert speed or torque, as in bicycles, clocks and cars. Perpendicular push is the normal force and restoring force is a spring.
t: Recall the function of each machine part.

x: All four are correct: pulleys lift loads in cranes, flagpoles and elevators, and gears are used in bicycles, clocks and automobiles.
t: Recall the uses of pulleys and gears.

x: Both are true: frictional heat lights a matchstick and also heats the drill during drilling.
t: Recall heat as a useful effect of friction.

x: The second law is F = ma: force equals mass times acceleration. The other options name different laws.
t: Recall the formula form of each law.

x: Statement A is true: vehicle design uses F = ma (the second law). Statement B is false: third-law examples are rockets, walking, swimming, recoil and jet engines.
t: Discriminate second-law from third-law applications.

x: Both are true and R explains A: balanced forces cause no change in motion, so a body stays at rest or keeps uniform velocity.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: The foot pushes the ground backward and the ground pushes the foot forward, which moves the walker. This is Newton's third law.
t: Recall that the reaction acts opposite to the action.

x: Both are true and R explains A: friction opposes the sliding of brake surfaces, and that opposition turns kinetic energy into heat.
t: Check whether R is the mechanism behind A.

x: Both are true: an unbalanced force changes the state of motion, which can mean slowing down or changing direction.
t: Recall that any change in speed or direction needs an unbalanced force.

x: Three are potential energy: electric, chemical and nuclear energy are stored. Thermal energy is internal energy from molecular motion.
t: Discriminate stored (potential) energy from energy of motion.

x: Both are true and R explains A: walking needs friction for the forward push, so without friction people slip.
t: Check whether R gives the cause of A.

x: All four are correct: the crowbar, bottle opener and human forearm are levers, and the screwdriver is a wheel and axle.
t: Recall the simple machine behind each tool.
